newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico hunger strike goes on despite crackdown.
newsitem.headline: Mexico hunger strike goes on despite crackdown.

text.p: A hunger strike by four Mexican street sweepers entered its 56th day on Monday despite a government crackdown the day before in which three other critically-weak protesters were forcibly taken to a hospital.

Defying Mexican police, who dispersed the protesters during a pre-dawn raid on Sunday, the four hunger strikers returned to a makeshift camp in southern Mexico City to continue the fast and demand their old jobs back.

Three other hunger strikers, including two who had survived on little more than water and glucose for 96 days, were forced into an ambulance and taken to a hospital during Sunday's crackdown. The government said it was a "humanitarian" move.

Medical officials said the prognosis on the health of all three was positive. But their colleagues were up in arms over the way they were treated, especially as the strikers had publically vowed to fast "to the death" just hours before they were hauled off to hospital against their will.

The hunger strikers are among 300 fired street sweepers from the southern state of Tabasco who have demanded better severance pay or rehiring. They said the drastic nature of the fast was justified by the extreme poverty of their families as a result of the job losses.
On Monday, President Ernesto Zedillo defended the decision to put the protesters in hospital, painting the hunger strikers as puppets of powerful protest leaders.
"Action was taken to prevent the fasters from dying and becoming victims of the shameless (protest) leaders," he said.
But the action, ordered by the Mexico City government led by Regent Oscar Espinosa, was roundly criticised by the opposition and some national newspapers.
The crackdown "will be remembered as one of the most deplorable and scandalous episodes in the life of the so-called regency," La Jornada said in a page-one editorial.
